title: When legal reasoning contradicts sports orthopaedic evidence.
journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA

sections.label: UNLABELED
sections.text: This manuscript presents the perspective of the International Society of Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) regarding a recent English High Court ruling that challenges established principles of evidence-based sports orthopaedic care. Following a legal case involving a professional footballer and the surgical management of an ankle fracture with concomitant arthroscopy, the authors highlight significant discrepancies between the legal conclusions and the current scientific literature. The ruling suggests that arthroscopic intervention contributed to the development of ankle arthritis and premature termination of the athlete's career. However, substantial evidence demonstrates that posttraumatic ankle arthritis is a well-recognised sequela of ankle fractures, particularly in the presence of prior injury and syndesmotic instability. Arthroscopy at the time of fracture fixation is widely regarded as the standard of care for identifying and managing intraarticular pathology. The judgement is critiqued for disregarding expert orthopaedic testimony, misinterpreting scientific evidence and endorsing unsupported theoretical mechanisms linking routine arthroscopic procedures to accelerated joint degeneration. The authors emphasise that such conclusions contradict accepted surgical practice and risk establishing harmful precedents that may deter appropriate management of similar injuries. This ICCRA statement highlights the need for alignment between medico-legal reasoning and scientific evidence to safeguard patient care and uphold the integrity of orthopaedic decision-making. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: NA.
